question: How many people died in the June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests?

sideA.label: KNCHR / Rights Groups
sideA.text: At least 60–63 people were killed nationwide between June and July 2024, per the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights' independent tally, most from police gunfire.

sideB.label: Government / Police
sideB.text: Officials initially cited far lower figures and disputed the KNCHR count, attributing some deaths to 'criminal elements' and looting rather than security-force action.

resolution: No single official reconciled figure exists; KNCHR's number of 60+ is the most widely cited by international media and rights groups, and later cumulative Amnesty tallies build on it.

question: Who set fire to sections of Parliament on June 25, 2024?

sideA.label: Protesters / Witnesses
sideA.text: Enraged demonstrators torched parliamentary offices after MPs passed the Finance Bill despite mass public opposition and days of warnings.

sideB.label: Government
sideB.text: Officials characterized the storming and arson as a coordinated, externally financed attempt to overthrow the government, not a spontaneous reaction.

resolution: Investigations and eyewitness accounts describe a spontaneous breach following police live fire on the crowd outside; no evidence of foreign financing behind the arson has been substantiated in court.

question: Who shot and killed Rex Masai?

sideA.label: Family / IPOA Inquest Witnesses
sideA.text: Video evidence shows a plainclothes officer firing into the crowd on Moi Avenue; the family says police have stonewalled efforts to identify him.

sideB.label: Police Leadership
sideB.text: A senior police officer testified investigators still did not know who fired the fatal shot, and denied that live bullets were used broadly against protesters.

resolution: As of the most recent inquest hearings, no officer had been charged in Masai's death more than a year after the shooting.

question: How did Albert Ojwang die in police custody?

sideA.label: Initial Police Account
sideA.text: Officers claimed Ojwang sustained fatal injuries by hitting his head against a cell wall.

sideB.label: Government Pathologist / Family
sideB.text: An independent autopsy found severe head trauma, neck compression and soft-tissue injuries consistent with assault and strangulation, not a self-inflicted injury.

resolution: The state's own pathologist contradicted the initial police account; two officers were arrested and Deputy IG Eliud Lagat stepped aside pending investigation.

question: How widespread were enforced disappearances of protesters?

sideA.label: Amnesty International
sideA.text: At least 83 enforced disappearances occurred alongside 128 killings and roughly 3,000 arrests across the 2024–2025 protest waves.

sideB.label: Government
sideB.text: Officials have denied any systematic policy of abductions, framing individual cases as isolated criminal matters under investigation rather than state policy.

resolution: KNCHR and Amnesty both documented dozens of unresolved disappearance cases; Amnesty traced officers involved to the DCI, Rapid Deployment Unit, Anti-Terrorism Police Unit and National Intelligence Service.

question: Did Interior CS Murkomen order police to shoot protesters?

sideA.label: Civil Society / Opposition
sideA.text: Murkomen's June 2025 remarks instructing police to shoot anyone approaching a police station amounted to an unconstitutional shoot-to-kill order that incited further violence.

sideB.label: Murkomen / Government
sideB.text: Murkomen said his comments were about protecting police stations from arson and mob attacks, not a general license to kill peaceful protesters, and partially clarified the remarks hours later.

resolution: A Milimani High Court petition sought to declare Murkomen unfit for office; as of August 2025 the court had declined to remove him but ordered him to respond to the allegations.

question: Were the 2024–2026 protests a coup attempt?

sideA.label: Ruto Administration
sideA.text: President Ruto and Interior CS Murkomen described the parliament storming and later unrest as a 'coup attempt' by 'treasonous anarchists' backed by unnamed financiers.

sideB.label: Protesters / Rights Groups
sideB.text: Organizers describe a leaderless, youth-led movement protesting tax policy, cost of living and police brutality, with no evidence of any plot to seize state power.

resolution: No coup-related charges leading to conviction have been substantiated in court; analysts widely view the 'coup' framing as a justification for the scale of the security crackdown.

question: Was activist Boniface Mwangi a terrorism financier?

sideA.label: DCI
sideA.text: Mwangi was arrested on July 19, 2025 and initially accused of facilitating terrorist activities during the June 25, 2025 protests.

sideB.label: Mwangi / Civil Society
sideB.text: Rights groups called the terrorism charge a pretext to criminalize dissent and intimidate a prominent critic, noting the case was quickly downgraded.

resolution: The state withdrew the terrorism charges days later and instead charged Mwangi with unlawful possession of ammunition, to which he pleaded not guilty on bail.

question: Does the Ruto–Raila 'broad-based government' represent the will of protesters?

sideA.label: Government / ODM
sideA.text: Ruto and Odinga presented the March 2025 KICC pact as a stabilizing, unifying arrangement that brings opposition figures into governance and reduces political tension.

sideB.label: Gen Z Movement / Public Opinion
sideB.text: Many Gen Z organizers reject the pact as elite power-sharing that co-opts opposition voices without addressing protester demands on accountability and cost of living.

resolution: A July 2026 TIFA poll found 52% of Kenyans opposed the broad-based government against 30% in support, suggesting the arrangement had not won broad public buy-in.

question: Is the Finance Act 2026 necessary fiscal reform or a repeat of 2024's mistakes?

sideA.label: Treasury / Government
sideA.text: Officials argue new levies, including on mobile money and betting, are required to close a widening revenue shortfall and slow the rise in Kenya's debt-to-GDP ratio.

sideB.label: Gen Z Organizers / Critics
sideB.text: Critics say taxing bread, mobile money and data again targets the same low-income and youth demographic that revolted in 2024, arguing the government 'learned nothing' from the uprising.

resolution: Parliament passed the bill 122–40 and Ruto signed it into law on June 23, 2026, days ahead of the protest anniversary, without major concessions on the contested levies.

question: Did police use live ammunition against peaceful protesters?

sideA.label: African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights / UN
sideA.text: The AU's human rights commission and UN human rights bodies deplored the use of live ammunition against unarmed, peaceful protesters across multiple protest dates.

sideB.label: Kenya Police Service
sideB.text: Police leadership maintains officers acted in self-defense against violent rioters and property destruction, and that force used was proportionate to the threat.

resolution: Independent autopsies in individual cases (Ojwang, Kariuki) and repeated international statements corroborate live-fire use; criminal prosecutions of officers remain limited relative to the documented death toll.

question: Was Gachagua's impeachment a genuine accountability process or political retaliation?

sideA.label: Parliament Majority
sideA.text: 291 MPs backed the impeachment motion, citing constitutional violations including corruption, ethnically divisive politics, and threatening a judge.

sideB.label: Gachagua / Allies
sideB.text: Gachagua called the impeachment an 'outrageous plot' to remove him for opposing government policy and for his continued sympathy toward some Gen Z grievances.

resolution: The Senate upheld several charges — including judicial intimidation and divisive politics — while clearing others, including corruption and money-laundering; Gachagua was removed and later formed his own political movement.

question: Did the government order a media blackout during the June 2025 anniversary protests?

sideA.label: Journalists / Press-Freedom Groups
sideA.text: Broadcasters reported being ordered to halt live coverage of the June 25, 2025 protests, which press-freedom advocates called unconstitutional censorship.

sideB.label: Government
sideB.text: Officials said any restrictions were aimed at preventing incitement and misinformation during active unrest, not a blanket ban on reporting.

resolution: Kenyan television and radio stations widely reported complying with an order to stop live broadcasts of the protests; the move drew condemnation from local and international press-freedom organizations.

question: How much will Finance Act 2026 raise the cost of mobile-money transfers?

sideA.label: Telecom Industry Estimates
sideA.text: Combined excise duty, transaction fees, and a new 16% VAT on payment service providers could push the total cost burden on M-Pesa transfers from 15% to as high as 33.4%.

sideB.label: Treasury
sideB.text: Government officials argue the new VAT applies to service-provider margins rather than being passed directly onto consumer transfer fees, and dispute the industry's cumulative-burden calculation.

resolution: As of the bill's passage, no independently verified figure for the final consumer-facing cost increase had been published; telecom operators continued warning of steep increases into mid-2026.

question: Is the 2026 unrest a genuine 'third wave' on the scale of 2024, or a smaller echo?

sideA.label: Government-Aligned Commentators
sideA.text: Officials point to the small Saba Saba 2026 crowd — described by one report as a 'tiny group' — as evidence the movement has lost momentum.

sideB.label: Organizers / Rights Groups
sideB.text: Organizers say heavy pre-emptive policing, road closures and hundreds of arrests suppressed turnout rather than reflecting any decline in public anger.

resolution: Both the near-total Nairobi CBD shutdown (business closures, 355+ arrests on June 25, 2026) and the sparse Saba Saba 2026 crowds are documented; analysts differ on whether this reflects fatigue, fear, or effective deterrence.

question: Why has the National Taskforce on Police Reforms report stayed unpublished for nearly three years?

sideA.label: David Maraga / Civil Society
sideA.text: Maraga, who chaired the taskforce, says the report — submitted to Ruto in November 2023 and prepared at public expense — contains recommendations to restore police independence and end brutality, and accuses the government of 'State Capture of the National Police Service' by sitting on it.

sideB.label: Government
sideB.text: The Ruto administration has not published the full report or offered a public timeline for its release, and had not responded to Maraga's August 2026 ultimatum as of the deadline.

resolution: Maraga's August 25, 2026 deadline expired without the government releasing the report or responding to his ultimatum; Maraga's threat to publish it independently remained outstanding. Two days later Ruto instead unveiled a redesigned police uniform, which commentators contrasted with the stalled substantive reforms.

question: Did Deputy President Kithure Kindiki know 2024 orders to abduct, torture or kill protesters were unconstitutional and fail to act?

sideA.label: Rigathi Gachagua
sideA.text: Gachagua says he personally challenged Kindiki, then Interior CS, after a National Security Council meeting, and that Kindiki privately agreed the proposed harsh measures against protesters were wrong but refused to confront President Ruto about them.

sideB.label: Kithure Kindiki
sideB.text: Kindiki dismissed the allegations as "petty lies," saying he was never directed to kill anyone and was focused on counterterrorism and banditry operations during the period in question.

resolution: No independent corroboration of either account has surfaced; the dispute plays out amid broader political tension between Gachagua and the Ruto administration following Gachagua's October 2024 impeachment.
